newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-PERMANENT MOVE TO NEW YORK HAS BEEN ON GRAF'S MIND.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-PERMANENT MOVE TO NEW YORK HAS BEEN ON GRAF'S MIND.

text.p: Tennis superstar Steffi Graf said on Friday that the emotional strain of her father's imprisonment and tax evasion trial has had her entertaining thoughts of giving up Germany as her home.
"There are times when I've been thinking about it, absolutely," Graf admitted, citing New York City as a possible alternative.
"I like to be at home," she said of her hometown of Bruhl. "I've got a lot of things that make it my home. But I definitely need my time away. That's why I was really desperate to come over."
The 27-year-old Graf was in New York, where she has kept an apartment for four years, to promote the WTA Tour's season-ending Chase Championships at Madison Square Garden.
But she was also here to get away from the strain of the trial.
"I've been there too long now and sometimes it can be pretty demanding and difficult," said Graf, who had been in Germany since shortly after winning the U.S. Open in September.
"With everything that's going on, sometimes it's easier to get away from it, just have a little distance," she said.
Peter Graf and family financial adviser Joachim Eckardt are on trial, charged with failing to pay taxes on several million dollars of Steffi's tennis earnings between 1989 and 1993.

Graf was apparently unaware that in Mannheim on Friday a German judge said the serious tax evasion charges might be downgraded, a move that could cut the maximum jail time if Peter Graf is found guilty in half to five years.

But that is just the latest twist in an emotional rollercoaster the tennis star has been on since her father was jailed back in August of 1995 on mere suspicion of failing to pay taxes. The charges were formally filed a year later.

Graf, who has been reduced to tears by questions on the subject in the past, handled herself with great poise when the trial came up during Friday's informal chat with reporters. She said she is not expecting to have to testify at the trial.

Dressed all in black and looking more like a fashion model than an athlete, a stylish Graf said she was dealing with the situation better, but admitted that the last few weeks had been especially difficult.

The trial judge in Mannheim had agreed to free her father on bail. But before Graf could be released, a higher court overturned the ruling, saying he posed a flight risk. Other attempts to get Peter Graf out of prison have also been thwarted.

"He's been close to it for so many times, and everything was arranged and suddenly they would say no," Graf said of the possible release of the man who had been her constant companion at tennis tournaments earlier in her career.
"The last six or seven weeks have been pretty turbulent in that. On and off constantly, they say yes, they say no.
"My brother flew over a few times and my mom (expecting his release) and every time, suddenly they say no, so it's been crazy," Graf said.
For the moment, Graf was just happy to be back in New York with its "thousands of great restaurants" and her "favorite cinema right around the corner."
Graf said she is often recognised when she walks around New York. "But in a nice way, in a gentle way," she said, dashing the stereotype of the pushy, obnoxious New Yorker.
"People in different countries approach you differently, in New York they are definitely respectful."
Then she sounded like a real native New Yorker herself.
"I'm upset about the parking situation like everybody else."
